sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why does a political party aim to achieve power? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) A political party is generally described as an organized body of people who share common principles and cherish certain common goals regarding the political system. Every political party pronounces its policies and programmes as commitment to the electorate. (2) The political parties seek power to form the government.

or.q: Why is the Indian party system called a multi-party system? Explain.
or.answer: (1) Many national, State and registered parties compete for power; no single party usually wins a majority, so national parties depend on regional parties and form coalition governments (NDA, UPA). (2) We can, therefore, say that democracy in India has been strengthened by a competitive and multi-party system. In general, the party system in India has not been a fixed one like a single party system or a dominant one-party system or a two-party system or a multiparty system.

questions.q: Explain any two major objectives of the Bharatiya Janata Party.
questions.answer: The BJP stands for (a) nationalism and national integration, (b) democracy, (c) positive secularism, (d) Gandhian socialism, and (e) value-based politics.

questions.q: Explain two characteristics of a political party.
questions.answer: (1) the organized group of people believe in common principles and common goals; (2) A political party operates and seeks political power through constitutional means to translate its policies into practice. it employs constitutional and peaceful methods in seeking control over the government through elections; and

questions.q: Mention the conditions required to be recognised as a national political party.
questions.answer: (1) Political parties in India are classified by the Election Commission for the allocation of symbols. In general, these groups try to press upon the government for formulation of policies or enactment of laws according to their interests. Some characteristics of interest groups, pressure groups and political parties are given below in a jumbled form. (2) It should be a recognized political party in four or more states. (3) It should have won at least 4 per cent of the seats in the last Lok Sabha elections or 3.33 per cent of the seats in the assembly elections from the state. All the candidates put by the party should have polled at least 6 per cent of the total valid votes in the elections.

questions.q: How do political parties help in running democratic processes?
questions.answer: (1) Political parties actually help the institutions and processes of a government democratic. They enable people to participate in elections and other processes of governance, educate them and facilitate them to make policy choices. (2) They place objectives and programmes before the voters through their manifestos; those securing the majority in elections form the government and enact and implement the policies; they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion.

questions.q: Why are Civil Society Organisations considered a new form of mass pressure tactics? Two points.
questions.answer: (1) Civil Society Organizations are formed by such vigilant citizens. These organizations are run by ordinary persons who feel strongly committed to certain issues. (2) Such organizations put pressure on the government for changing policies on many important issues such as corruption, human rights, livelihood of different people, environmental protection, women empowerment, educational and health issues. They point out when the government is not fulfilling its promises to the nation.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain any three challenges faced by political parties in India.
questions.answer: (1) Lack of internal democracy and dynastic succession — power stays with a few leaders and families. (2) Growing role of money and muscle power and criminalisation of politics. (3) Coalition compulsions and frequent switching of alliances make parties focus on short-term gains and emotive issues rather than ideology and lasting policies.

questions.q: Explain, with examples, the role of pressure groups.
questions.answer: (1) they educate people and help in formulating and shaping public opinion; For example, the trade unions help their respective political parties by providing them workers during elections. They help promote, discuss, debate and mobilize public opinion on major public issues. (2) They press the government through petitions, lobbying, demonstrations, satyagraha and strikes — e.g. FICCI on industrial policy, Kisan Sabhas on farm prices. (3) These groups try to bring changes in public policy. For instance, the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) has influenced the government to improve its policies on the rights of women workers. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan led the people’s movement which got the government to bring about the law on ‘Right to Information’.

questions.q: Differentiate between national and regional political parties with examples.
questions.answer: (1) A national party should be a recognized political party in four or more states. National Parties- 7 (Congress, BJP, CPM, CPI, BSP, Nationalist Congress Party and Rashtriya Janata Dal). (2) Regional political parties have emerged to fulfill regional aspirations. The regional political parties include, among others, the Akali Dal (Punjab), the DMK and the AIADMK (Tamil Nadu), the Telugu Desam (Andhra Pradesh), the National Conference (Jammu and Kashmir), the Shiv Sena (Maharashtra), the Trinamool Congress (West Bengal). (3) National parties take up national and international issues, while regional parties focus on their State's interests and often support coalitions at the Centre.

questions.q: How are pressure groups different from political parties? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Pressure groups are not primarily political in nature. The political parties seek power to form the government. (2) Pressure groups do not necessarily have political ideologies. Political parties nominate candidates, contest elections, and participate in elections campaigns. (3) Pressure groups have specific, limited interests and may have no ideology; parties have ideologies and broad national programmes.

questions.q: Differentiate between pressure groups and interest groups.
questions.answer: (1) These are called pressure groups or interest groups. An interest group that exerts pressure on the government to achieve its goals is called a pressure group. A pressure group is an interest group which exerts pressure on the government or the decision-makers for the fulfillment of the interests of its members. (2) Pressure groups do not necessarily have political ideologies. (3) Interest groups are softer and more protective; pressure groups are strictly structured, harsher and both protective and promotive. All pressure groups are interest groups, but not all interest groups are pressure groups.

questions.q: Explain the importance of regional political parties in India.
questions.answer: (1) Regional political parties have emerged to fulfill regional aspirations. (2) The regional political parties have come to play a vital role in the formation of governments at the Centre. (3) It is because of the regional political parties that our party-system has been federalized. The evolving nature of our party system has strengthened the cooperative trends of our federal system.

or.q: What are Civil Society Organisations? Write the names of any four contemporary Civil Society Organisations in India.
or.answer: (1) CSOs are associations, groups and voluntary agencies formed by citizens to pursue issues of common concern — environment, corruption, price rise, gender justice, child labour — acting as an interface between the State and the individual and pressing the government to change policies. (2) Some important leaders of Civil Society Organizations in recent times include Aruna Roy (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan), Ela Bhatt (Self-employed Women’s Association), Medha Patkar (Narmada Bachao Andolan) and Anna Hazare (India Against Corruption).

questions.q: Suggest any six effective measures to reform political parties.
questions.answer: (1) Ensure internal democracy — regular organisational elections within parties. (2) Make party finances transparent and audit them; limit election expenses. (3) Keep candidates with criminal records out of elections. (4) Enforce the anti-defection law to stop party-switching for gain. (5) Give fair representation to women and weaker sections in tickets and posts. (6) Encourage parties to campaign on policies and programmes rather than caste, religion and emotive slogans, and let citizens and the media keep a check.
